data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Independent operation does not imply independent failure: the distinguishing evidence is whether operators share a common dependency graph, and truly independent failures require provably disjoint dependency graphs, not merely separate management.","counterconditions":[{"case":"Decentralized operators can and do coordinate to ensure disjoint dependency graphs without losing operational independence","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The large service cannot achieve truly disjoint internal dependency graphs due to cost or complexity constraints","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"Dependency graph overlap is not the primary driver of correlated failure; other mechanisms dominate","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Two independently operated services can still share all their critical dependencies (same cloud region, same CDN, same TLS certificate authority). Their failures appear uncorrelated until the shared dependency fails, at which point they fail together. The causal mechanism for distinguishing truly independent failures from merely uncorrelated ones is the dependency graph: failures are truly independent only if the dependency graphs are provably disjoint (no shared power, network, software, or data dependencies). A large service with internally enforced diversity can have disjoint dependency graphs by design, while decentralized operators cannot guarantee this without coordination that undermines their independence.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
